assumptions.label: Equity real return
assumptions.basis: Long-run US equity real return has run ~6.5-7%; this trims it for today's starting valuations and for fees/slippage. Not a forecast — a planning number.

assumptions.label: Equity volatility
assumptions.basis: Annual standard deviation of a broad equity index, close to the long-run realised figure.

assumptions.label: Bond real return
assumptions.basis: Real yield available on intermediate high-grade bonds, held to maturity. Positive but thin.

assumptions.label: Bond volatility
assumptions.basis: Annual standard deviation of an intermediate bond index. Higher than the pre-2022 assumption for a reason.

assumptions.label: Cash real return
assumptions.basis: Cash is assumed to match inflation and no more. Over long windows it has often done slightly worse.

assumptions.label: Equity/bond correlation
assumptions.basis: Modestly positive. The negative correlation of 1990-2020 was a regime, not a law, and 2022 showed both sides falling together.

assumptions.label: General inflation
assumptions.basis: Slightly above the 2% target because the plan should survive the overshoot, not the target.

assumptions.label: Healthcare inflation
assumptions.basis: Medical costs have persistently outrun general inflation. Applied only to the healthcare line, never to total spending.

assumptions.label: Education inflation
assumptions.basis: Tuition has outrun general inflation for decades in both the US and urban India.

assumptions.label: Planning horizon (self)
assumptions.basis: A planning age, not a life expectancy. Roughly the 85th percentile survival age for a healthy person now in their 40s — you plan for the tail, not the median, because the median outcome is the one you can afford to be wrong about.

assumptions.label: Planning horizon (spouse)
assumptions.basis: Set higher than the primary horizon: for a couple, the money has to last until the SECOND death, and female life expectancy runs longer.

assumptions.label: Baseline withdrawal rate
assumptions.basis: Below the classic 4% because that study assumed a 30-year US retirement, a 50/50 portfolio and no fees. A retirement starting before 60 is longer than 30 years.

assumptions.label: USD/INR drift
assumptions.basis: Long-run rupee depreciation against the dollar, roughly the inflation differential. Directionally reliable, annually useless.

assumptions.label: Real salary growth
assumptions.basis: Above-inflation raises, net of the fact that they stop or reverse late in a career.

assumptions.label: Monte Carlo paths
assumptions.basis: Enough that the success probability is stable to well under a percentage point between runs.

rows.note: The classic rule. Assumes a 30-year retirement; the study it comes from never claimed more. Your horizon is ~47 years, so this rate is being used outside the evidence it rests on.
Reasonable for a 35-40 year horizon with a globally diversified portfolio and some spending flexibility.
Appropriate for a retirement of 40+ years, or for someone who cannot cut spending in a bad decade.
Close to a perpetual-endowment rate. Survives almost any history, and costs the most years of work to reach.

B.note: Essentials funded at 3.00% so they survive a bad sequence; lifestyle at 5.0% because it can be cut. Requires you to actually cut it.

buckets.name: Bucket 1 — years 0-3
buckets.why: Three years of spending that never has to be sold into a down market.

buckets.name: Bucket 2 — years 3-10
buckets.why: Refills Bucket 1. Long enough to ride out a typical recession without touching equities.

buckets.name: Bucket 3 — years 10+
buckets.why: Present value of years 10-47 of spending, discounted at 2.7% real.

C.note: Sized from spending, not from a target allocation — the equity share falls out of the arithmetic. Reads lower than Models A and B because it is allowed to hit zero at age 47 years from retirement; those two are sized to last indefinitely.

D.note: Start at 4.25%. If the withdrawal rate rises past 5.10% (portfolio down), cut spending 10%; if it falls below 3.40%, a raise is affordable. After two consecutive cuts you would be living on $2,400.

withdrawal_models.interpretation: A moderate spread. Which model you follow matters, but no choice among them is catastrophic.

rungs.note: Essentials only — housing, food, healthcare, insurance, taxes. The line below which the plan is fragile.
Life continues exactly as it does today.
Today's spending +25%. A convention, not a finding.
Today's spending +60%. Flexibility for family support and bad years.

next_rung.note: Essentials only — housing, food, healthcare, insurance, taxes. The line below which the plan is fragile.

fi_ladder.basis: Required capital = annual spending ÷ 3.50%. Real terms, before any tax on withdrawals.

earliest_caveat: Deterministic: assumes the expected return every year, with no bad sequence. Treat it as the optimistic edge of the range, not as a date.

rows.label: Aggressive (deterministic)
rows.basis: Expected return every year, no bad sequence.

rows.label: Financially safe (80% survival)
rows.basis: 98% of simulated sequences last the full horizon.

rows.label: Safe with spending flexibility
rows.basis: 80% survival, given a willingness to cut discretionary spending when a guardrail is breached.

timeline.note: The spread between these ages is not error — it is the plan's sensitivity to luck. A narrow spread means the date is robust; a wide one means it depends on the sequence you happen to get.

monte_carlo.caveat: Independent normal real returns, no taxes, no inflation shock. A model result, not a forecast.

monte_carlo_flexible.caveat: Independent normal real returns, no taxes, no inflation shock. A model result, not a forecast.

scenarios.title: Lost decade
scenarios.blurb: Ten years of roughly zero real return, starting at retirement.

scenarios.title: 2008-style crash
scenarios.blurb: A 45% drawdown five years before retirement, then recovery.

scenarios.title: 2020-style crash
scenarios.blurb: A 34% drawdown and a fast, complete recovery.

scenarios.title: High inflation
scenarios.blurb: Inflation runs hot for a decade: real returns compress and real spending rises.

scenarios.title: Low returns + high inflation
scenarios.blurb: The worst combination — depressed real returns for the whole horizon.

scenarios.title: Crash immediately after retiring
scenarios.blurb: A 35% drawdown in the first year of retirement, then recovery.

scenarios.verdict: The plan survives all eight histories. That is a strong result — and it is a deterministic one, so read it alongside the Monte Carlo probability, not instead of it.
